'''''Prunus campanulata''''' is a species of [[cherry]] native to Japan, Taiwan, southern and eastern China (Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan, Hunan, Fujian, and Zhejiang), and Vietnam.<ref name=FoC/> It is a large shrub or small tree, growing {{cvt|3|-|8|m|0}} tall.<ref name=FoC/> It is widely grown as an [[ornamental tree]], and a symbol of [[Nago, Okinawa|Nago]] in the [[Ryukyu Islands]] of [[Japan]]. It is variously known in [[English (language)|English]] as the '''Taiwan cherry''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 10 January 2018}}</ref> '''Formosan cherry''', or '''bellflower cherry'''. It was described in 1883 by [[Carl Johann Maximowicz]].<ref name=ipni1/>

==Invasive species==
The tree is an [[invasive plant species]] in some areas of New Zealand.<ref>https://www.nzherald.co.nz/northern-advocate/news/whangarei-council-called-out-for-unchecked-taiwanese-cherry-trees/DC2L7YWK4FFKLJYUU7TM22TCZI/</ref> In the [[Northland Region]] of New Zealand it is illegal to distribute, sell or propagate the plant or to distribute soil, gravel, etc., that contain the seeds or other parts of the plant.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nrc.govt.nz/upload/2412/Community%20Pest%20Plant%20Control%20Areas.pdf |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721234457/http://www.nrc.govt.nz/upload/2412/Community%20Pest%20Plant%20Control%20Areas.pdf |archivedate=21 July 2011 |title=Northland Pest Management Strategy |publisher=Northland Regional Council |accessdate=12 August 2010}}</ref>

==Ecological interactions==
''Prunus campanulata'' is the host of larval ''[[Chrysozephyrus nishikaze]]'', a butterfly species [[endemic]] to Taiwan.<ref name="Savela"/> Flowers and nectar of ''Prunus campanulata'' are among the main food sources of [[Taiwan yuhina]]s during their breeding season.<ref name="Lee et al. 2005"/>

==Reproduction==
''Prunus campanulata'' is one of the many cherry blossom trees that blooms early. Their seeds portray a physiological and morphological dormancy that is broken when exposed to cold and warm temperatures before germination. The flower is fertilized by pollinating insects and can begin to flower in 1 to 2 years.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

== Cultivars ==
In Japan, a large number of [[cultivar]]s have been developed from this species through both natural hybridization with other species and intentional crossbreeding. Among these, the earliest to become widespread and the most representative are ''Prunus × kanzakura'' 'Kawazu-zakura' and ''Prunus'' 'Yoko'. Both are popular for their distinctly deep pink petals and early flowering period, traits influenced by the genetic characteristics of this species, which clearly distinguish them from [[Prunus × yedoensis|Somei-yoshino]], the most widely known cherry tree.<ref name ="katsuki2015">{{Cite book|first=Toshio |last=Katsuki |date=2015|title=Sakura |publisher=[[Iwanami Shoten]] |isbn=978-4-00-431534-6 |language=ja }}</ref>{{Rp|pages=98–100, 221}} However, unlike this species, neither exhibits the characteristic bell-shaped flowers; instead, they produce much larger blossoms and differ in flowering season.<ref name="hkawazu"/><ref name="hyoko"/>

=== Kawazu-zakura ===
'Kawazu-zakura' originated around 1950 from a wild seedling discovered along the Kawazu River in [[Kawazu, Shizuoka|Kawazu]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], which was cultivated at the residence of Michinobu Iida and later developed into a named cultivar. The original tree is still extant. It is considered to have arisen from an interspecific hybrid, likely through natural hybridization with [[Prunus speciosa|Oshima cherry]]. Flowering from late February to early March, it blooms significantly earlier than most cherry trees, and the rows of trees along the river have become a major tourist attraction in the town.<ref name ="katsuki2015"/>{{Rp|pages=98–100, 221}}<ref name="hkawazu">{{cite web|url=https://www.hananokai.or.jp/sakura-zukan/kawaduzakura/?n[]=1396|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250326155130/https://www.hananokai.or.jp/sakura-zukan/kawaduzakura/?n[]=1396|title=Kawazu-zakura|publisher=The Flower Association of Japan|date=|archive-date=26 March 2025|access-date=30 March 2026}}</ref>

=== Yoko ===
'Yoko', meaning "sunlight," was developed in 1981 by Masaaki Takaoka, the founder and first president of Hakata Salt Co., Ltd., who resided in [[Tōon, Ehime|Tōon]], [[Ehime Prefecture]]. After 25 years of trial and error, he selected it from progeny obtained by crossing '[[Prunus × yedoensis#Other cultivars|Amagi-yoshino]]' with this species.<ref name="hyoko">{{cite web|url=https://www.hananokai.or.jp/sakura-zukan/yoko/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260114205729/https://www.hananokai.or.jp/sakura-zukan/yoko/|title=Yoko|publisher=The Flower Association of Japan|date=|archive-date=14 January 2026|access-date=30 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hakatanoshio.co.jp/news/blog/news/news_125.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210320131610/https://www.hakatanoshio.co.jp/news/blog/news/news_125.html|title=「陽光」桜の父、初代高岡社長の顕彰碑が建てられました|publisher=Hakata Salt Co., Ltd.|date=|archive-date=20 March 2021|access-date=30 March 2026}}</ref> It is a cultivar noted for its resistance to [[Witch's broom]] disease.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.koutou-nouen.com/cgi-bin/cargo/goodsprev.cgi?gno=sa07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170404043906/http://www.koutou-nouen.com/cgi-bin/cargo/goodsprev.cgi?gno=sa07|title=陽光桜 ようこうさくら（接ぎ木・素掘り）【1年生】|publisher=Koutou Nouen|date=|archive-date=4 April 2017|access-date=30 March 2026}}</ref>
